newsitem.title: USA: White House sees "persuasive case" on Barshefsky.
newsitem.headline: White House sees "persuasive case" on Barshefsky.

text.p: The White House said Monday it believed the administration can make a persuasive case that Charlene Barshefsky, President Bill Clinton's nominee to be U.S. Trade Representative, should be exempt from a law that would bar her from the position because of her past work.

"I've seen some comments from people express some concern, but we think we can make a persuasive case," spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters when asked if he forsaw any problem in Barshefsky's being confirmed by the U.S. Senate.
"Certainly the quality of the nominee herself is the strongest argument for the exemption," McCurry added.

A law passed in 1995 would bar Barshefsky from being elevated to the trade representative's job because she briefly advised Canada as a private attorney in 1990 on a dispute it had with the United States over lumber.
Clinton on Wednesday asked Congress to pass a waiver to the law clearing the way for Barshefsky's confirmation.
McCurry said the White House had "had some some productive discussions so far" with Congress on the waiver, adding: "We hope it's expeditiously and favorably received."
Barshefsky was deputy to U.S. Trade Representative Mickey Kantor and last year was elevated to the top job on an acting basis when Kantor replaced late Commerce Secretary Ron Brown.
